sentences.text: This animal was a medium-sized member of the mosasaur family, with the largest known species reaching lengths of 5.5 meters.
Despite possessing a relatively short skull, the creature featured proportionally larger eyes than many of its relatives.
Its jaws held fewer teeth than most other mosasaurs, consisting of only about 12 large, curved structures.
The genus was first discovered in Europe by paleontologist Louis Dollo in the year 1882.
Edward Drinker Cope found a specimen in North America in 1869 that was initially identified as Mosasaurus but was later reclassified as Plioplatecarpus in 1870.
Fossils have been found in the Pierre Shale of Kansas, Demopolis Chalk of Alabama, Mississippi, North Dakota, South Dakota, Canada, Sweden, the Netherlands, and Wyoming.
Researchers suggest the larger eyes of this animal may be an adaptation to low-light conditions in deeper water.
The greatly recurved teeth suggest it hunted relatively small prey that it could grasp precisely.
The wide distribution of fossils in North America and Europe suggests Plioplatecarpus was an open ocean predator.
A 1999 study described a specimen from a non-marine deposit, suggesting Plioplatecarpus might have entered freshwater and estuarine habitats.
The genus Plioplatecarpus includes the type species P. marshi described by Dollo in 1882, along with other species such as P. depressus, P. primaevus, P. houzeaui, and P. peckensis.
The genus Oterognathus is a synonym of Plioplatecarpus.
Plioplatecarpus belongs to the subfamily Plioplatecarpinae.
Phosphorosaurus is another synonym of the genus Plioplatecarpus.
Plioplatecarpus lived during the late Cretaceous period, approximately 82 to 68 million years ago.
Plioplatecarpus lived in the Upper Cretaceous, about 83.5 million years ago.
The fossil record for Plioplatecarpus spans from the Cenomanian to the Danian stages, between 100.5 and 61.66 million years ago.
